title: Science Fiction
description: Wells to Le Guin to Liu Cixin — speculation as literature

concepts.title: Origins
concepts.contentHtml:
Science fiction as a recognisable genre emerged in the late 19th century. Mary Shelley's Frankenstein (1818) is the standard point of origin, fusing Romantic gothic with scientific anxiety. Jules Verne (1828-1905) and H.G. Wells (1866-1946) institutionalised the form: Verne's voyages and machines, Wells's The Time Machine, The War of the Worlds, The Invisible Man.

The pulp magazines of the 1920s-1940s (Amazing Stories from 1926, Astounding under John W. Campbell from 1937) created the genre community. Asimov, Heinlein, Clarke emerged from this environment.

concepts.title: Golden Age and New Wave
concepts.contentHtml:
The Golden Age (roughly 1938-1960) under Campbell emphasised hard science, problem-solving heroes, and confidence in technology. Asimov's robot stories and Foundation series, Heinlein's juvenile novels, Clarke's Childhood's End.

The New Wave (1960s-70s) reacted against this. Michael Moorcock's New Worlds magazine in Britain, Harlan Ellison's Dangerous Visions anthology in the US. Stylistic experimentation, social and psychological themes, abandoning Campbell's optimism. J.G. Ballard, Ursula K. Le Guin, Samuel Delany, Joanna Russ.

concepts.title: Le Guin and the Soft Sciences
concepts.contentHtml:
Ursula K. Le Guin (1929-2018) opened the genre to anthropology, sociology, gender, and politics. The Left Hand of Darkness (1969) imagined a world of androgynous beings. The Dispossessed (1974) compared a capitalist and an anarchist society. The Lathe of Heaven, the Earthsea series, the Hainish cycle.

Her work showed the genre could be philosophically and politically serious without abandoning the speculative premise. Many later writers — Octavia Butler, Margaret Atwood, Kim Stanley Robinson — work in the space she opened.

concepts.title: Cyberpunk and Beyond
concepts.contentHtml:
Cyberpunk emerged in the 1980s. William Gibson's Neuromancer (1984) is the founding text — gritty near-future, virtual reality, multinational corporations, body modification, hacker protagonists. Bruce Sterling, Pat Cadigan, Neal Stephenson followed.

The 1990s and 2000s diversified: alternate history (Philip K. Dick's earlier work, The Yiddish Policemen's Union); literary SF (Atwood, Ishiguro's Never Let Me Go); New Weird (China Miéville). The genre's old boundaries — fantasy, horror, literary fiction — eroded.

concepts.title: Global SF
concepts.contentHtml:
21st-century SF is increasingly global. Liu Cixin's The Three-Body Problem (2008, English 2014) brought Chinese SF to international attention. Cixin Liu, Ken Liu (also a major translator), Hao Jingfang represent the Chinese flowering.

Octavia Butler, N.K. Jemisin, Tochi Onyebuchi extended Black SF traditions. Nnedi Okorafor brought West African material into the genre. Ted Chiang's philosophically dense short fiction has been widely celebrated.

The genre has become one of the most generative spaces for thinking about climate, technology, and the future. Atwood resists the SF label for her work; many readers ignore the resistance.

title: Fantasy
description: Tolkien, Le Guin, the second worlds

concepts.title: Roots
concepts.contentHtml:
Modern fantasy descends from multiple traditions: classical and Norse mythology, fairy tales, medieval romance, the Gothic novel. George MacDonald's Phantastes (1858) and William Morris's late prose romances are 19th-century precursors. Lord Dunsany's The Gods of Pegāna (1905) and Edgar Rice Burroughs's John Carter of Mars books shaped the early 20th century.

The 1920s-1930s pulp magazines produced Robert E. Howard's Conan stories — sword and sorcery as a distinct mode — and H.P. Lovecraft's cosmic horror, which crosses into fantasy territory.

concepts.title: Tolkien
concepts.contentHtml:
J.R.R. Tolkien (1892-1973), an Oxford professor of Old English, transformed fantasy with The Hobbit (1937) and The Lord of the Rings (1954-55).

His distinctive contribution: worldbuilding at unprecedented depth. Middle-earth has invented languages with worked-out grammars (Elvish), a thousand-year history, multiple cultures, a creation mythology. The novel's surface plot rests on a vast underlying construction.

Tolkien's influence is enormous. Most epic fantasy since 1970 — Terry Brooks, Stephen Donaldson, Robert Jordan, George R.R. Martin, Brandon Sanderson — descends from him. The genre's expectations about secondary worlds are largely his.

concepts.title: Le Guin and Earthsea
concepts.contentHtml:
Ursula K. Le Guin's A Wizard of Earthsea (1968) and the subsequent Earthsea books offered an alternative to Tolkien.

Smaller in scope but deeper in psychological focus. The protagonist's journey is one of self-recognition rather than world-saving combat. The series increasingly engaged feminist and anti-colonial themes (Tehanu, 1990, returned to Earthsea explicitly to revise the early books' male-centred assumptions).

Le Guin's essays on fantasy and SF, collected in The Language of the Night, remain among the most thoughtful arguments for taking the genre seriously.

concepts.title: After Tolkien
concepts.contentHtml:
The post-Tolkien decades have seen continuous reworking.

Grimdark: George R.R. Martin's A Song of Ice and Fire (1996-) introduced moral ambiguity, no-character-is-safe plotting, and political realism into epic fantasy. The HBO adaptation made Martin's vision globally famous.

Urban fantasy: Neil Gaiman's American Gods (2001), Susanna Clarke's Jonathan Strange & Mr Norrell (2004), the Charles de Lint and Holly Black traditions. Magic intersecting modern life.

The New Weird: China Miéville's Perdido Street Station (2000), Jeff VanderMeer's Annihilation (2014). Genre boundaries deliberately blurred.

Diverse voices: N.K. Jemisin's Broken Earth trilogy (2015-17, three consecutive Hugos), Tomi Adeyemi, Rebecca Roanhorse, R.F. Kuang.

concepts.title: Why Fantasy Persists
concepts.contentHtml:
Fantasy is the bestselling fiction genre in many years. Why?

It allows direct engagement with mythic and ethical material that realist fiction handles only obliquely. Quests, choices, transformations, evil-confronted-and-overcome: the patterns that myth has always served are still wanted.

It permits worldbuilding as an aesthetic in its own right. Readers come to fantasy partly for the pleasure of inhabiting elaborated invented worlds.

It allows political analogy at protected distance. Tolkien wrote about industrialism and total war; Le Guin about colonialism and gender; Jemisin about racial oppression. The fantasy frame lets these themes be developed with unusual freedom.

The genre has moved from cultural ghetto to mainstream prestige in fifty years. The trajectory is unlikely to reverse.

title: Mystery & Crime
description: Poe, Conan Doyle, Christie, Highsmith, Chandler

concepts.title: Origins of Detection
concepts.contentHtml:
The detective story begins with Edgar Allan Poe. Three stories featuring C. Auguste Dupin — 'The Murders in the Rue Morgue' (1841), 'The Mystery of Marie Rogêt' (1842), 'The Purloined Letter' (1844) — established the form's basic conventions: a crime that puzzles ordinary intelligence, a brilliant outsider detective, a less brilliant companion-narrator, ratiocination as the path to solution.

Poe's own contribution was small in volume; his influence was enormous. Every later detective story is partly a response to him.

concepts.title: Holmes
concepts.contentHtml:
Arthur Conan Doyle's Sherlock Holmes — debuting in A Study in Scarlet (1887), running through 56 stories and 4 novels — became the most famous fictional detective ever.

The combination of an eccentric superior intelligence (Holmes) with a more average narrator (Watson) became the genre template. Holmes's deductive method — observing details others miss, reconstructing causes from effects — has been imitated, parodied, and updated continuously.

The character's afterlife has been remarkable. He was killed off in 1893 and brought back by public demand in 1901-02. Adaptations across film, TV, and other media have continued every decade since.

concepts.title: The Golden Age
concepts.contentHtml:
Between WWI and WWII, the British Golden Age of detective fiction produced the puzzle novel at its peak. Agatha Christie (1890-1976) wrote 66 novels, 14 short story collections, and the longest-running play in history (The Mousetrap, 1952). Poirot and Miss Marple are her famous detectives.

Other Golden Age figures: Dorothy L. Sayers (Lord Peter Wimsey), Ngaio Marsh, Margery Allingham, John Dickson Carr (locked-room mysteries). The 'fair play' principle held: clues must be available to the reader before the solution is revealed.

Christie remains, by some metrics, the bestselling novelist of all time. Her plotting ingenuity — the trick endings of And Then There Were None, The Murder of Roger Ackroyd — has been imitated for a century.

concepts.title: Hardboiled
concepts.contentHtml:
Across the Atlantic, the American hardboiled tradition emerged in the same period. Dashiell Hammett's The Maltese Falcon (1930) and Raymond Chandler's Philip Marlowe novels (The Big Sleep, 1939, onward) established its conventions.

Where Christie's mysteries were intellectual puzzles in country houses, hardboiled fiction was set in cities, dealt with corruption, violence, and moral ambiguity, and featured wisecracking working-class detectives. Chandler's prose — wry, metaphor-rich — became a major American literary style in its own right.

The hardboiled tradition led to noir, in which the detective often becomes ensnared in the corruption rather than escaping it. Jim Thompson, James M. Cain, David Goodis. Patricia Highsmith's amoral Tom Ripley novels (1955-91) extended the noir mode into psychological territory.

concepts.title: Contemporary Crime
concepts.contentHtml:
The genre has continued to expand and diversify.

Police procedural: Ed McBain's 87th Precinct (1956-2005), Michael Connelly, Henning Mankell. The detective embedded in actual police work.

Nordic noir: Stieg Larsson's The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo trilogy, Jo Nesbø, Karin Fossum. The tradition has been globally exported.

Literary crime: P.D. James, Tana French, Kate Atkinson, John Banville (writing as Benjamin Black). Crime as a vehicle for literary ambition.

Diverse voices: Walter Mosley's Easy Rawlins, Sara Paretsky's V.I. Warshawski, Attica Locke. Crime fiction interrogating American history.

The mystery and crime genres have produced more readable consistently strong fiction over the past century than any other category.

title: Horror
description: Shelley, Stoker, Lovecraft, King — fear as form

concepts.title: Gothic Beginnings
concepts.contentHtml:
Horror as a genre descends from the late-18th-century Gothic novel. Horace Walpole's The Castle of Otranto (1764), Ann Radcliffe's The Mysteries of Udolpho (1794), Matthew Lewis's The Monk (1796) established the conventions: ruined castles, supernatural threats, persecuted heroines, atmospheric dread.

Mary Shelley's Frankenstein (1818) and the various 19th-century Gothic — Hogg's Confessions of a Justified Sinner, Stevenson's Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde, Wilde's The Picture of Dorian Gray — extended the form. Bram Stoker's Dracula (1897) gave the vampire its modern shape.

concepts.title: Lovecraft and Cosmic Horror
concepts.contentHtml:
H.P. Lovecraft (1890-1937) developed cosmic horror: the suggestion that the universe is governed by indifferent or malevolent forces beyond human comprehension. His Cthulhu mythos became one of the most influential fictional cosmologies of the 20th century.

Lovecraft's prose can be purple, his racism is undeniable and a legitimate problem, but his core insight — horror as the recognition of human cosmic insignificance — has been extended by writers including Caitlín R. Kiernan, Laird Barron, Thomas Ligotti, and Victor LaValle (whose The Ballad of Black Tom, 2016, directly engages and revises Lovecraft's racial politics).

concepts.title: The Modern Horror Novel
concepts.contentHtml:
Mid-20th-century horror diversified. Shirley Jackson's The Haunting of Hill House (1959) and We Have Always Lived in the Castle (1962) developed psychological horror at literary intensity. Richard Matheson's I Am Legend (1954) modernised the vampire tradition.

Stephen King (b. 1947) became the dominant horror novelist of the late 20th century. Carrie, The Shining, It, The Stand, Misery, Pet Sematary. King's combination of supernatural premise with sharply observed American small-town realism became the genre's commercial template.

Other major figures: Clive Barker, Peter Straub, Anne Rice (whose vampire novels redefined the figure), Tananarive Due.

concepts.title: Subgenres and Modes
concepts.contentHtml:
Horror has many sub-modes.

Body horror: focused on physical transformation and disgust. Cronenberg's films, Junji Ito's manga, parts of Clive Barker.

Folk horror: ancient rural rituals and survivals breaking into modern life. The Wicker Man (1973), Midsommar (2019), Andrew Michael Hurley's The Loney.

Slasher: more cinematic than literary, but Jack Ketchum's The Girl Next Door represents the literary equivalent.

Quiet horror / weird fiction: emphasising atmosphere over shock. Robert Aickman, Helen Oyeyemi, Mariana Enriquez.

Apocalyptic horror: The Road (Cormac McCarthy), Justin Cronin's The Passage.

concepts.title: Why Horror
concepts.contentHtml:
Why do readers want to be frightened?

Theories: catharsis (releasing real anxieties safely), control (mastering fear in the controlled space of the page), exploration of taboo (death, violation, transformation), confrontation with the limits of meaning.

The genre also serves diagnostic functions. Horror often surfaces what culture would prefer to repress — racial guilt (Jordan Peele's films, Toni Morrison's Beloved), sexual trauma, environmental dread, technological anxiety. The unspeakable speaks through the genre's protected fictional frame.

Contemporary horror has gained literary respect. The 'elevated horror' label (sometimes used dismissively) marks the integration of horror conventions into prestige fiction. Carmen Maria Machado, Stephen Graham Jones, Mariana Enriquez are all both horror writers and literary writers — the boundary has effectively dissolved.

title: Romance
description: From Austen to today's mass market — desire on the page

concepts.title: What Romance Is
concepts.contentHtml:
Romance as a contemporary genre is fiction centred on a love story with an emotionally satisfying ending — the Romance Writers of America's official definition specifies an HEA (Happily Ever After) or HFN (Happy For Now) ending.

This is distinct from love stories that end tragically (Madame Bovary, Anna Karenina) or unsettlingly (Lolita). Genre romance has rules. The reader's pleasure is partly the assurance that the central relationship will, after obstacles, succeed.

The genre is by far the largest category of fiction by sales. It outsells thrillers, mysteries, and literary fiction combined in many years.

concepts.title: Origins
concepts.contentHtml:
The romance genre's roots run through medieval romance (chivalric love stories), Renaissance prose romance, the 18th-century epistolary novel (Richardson's Pamela), and the 19th-century novel — particularly Austen and the Brontës.

Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice (1813) is in some sense the foundational modern romance: courtship plot, witty heroine, eventual reconciliation with proud hero, satisfying happy ending. Generations of romance novels work the Darcy template.

Georgette Heyer's Regency romances (1921-74) created the Regency subgenre, which has remained a romance staple. Daphne du Maurier's Rebecca (1938) blended romance with gothic.

concepts.title: Mass-Market Romance
concepts.contentHtml:
The modern mass-market romance dates from Harlequin's post-WWII expansion. Founded 1949, Harlequin became the dominant romance publisher in the second half of the 20th century, with category lines (Harlequin Romance, Harlequin Presents, Harlequin Desire) targeting specific reader preferences.

The 1970s and 1980s saw Kathleen Woodiwiss's The Flame and the Flower (1972) introduce more explicit sexuality. Nora Roberts (b. 1950) became the bestselling romance novelist of all time.

The genre has been condescended to but has been technically and economically central to publishing for half a century. Romance readers buy more books per capita than readers of any other genre.

concepts.title: Subgenres
concepts.contentHtml:
Contemporary romance is highly fragmented by subgenre.

Historical (especially Regency, Victorian, Scottish): Julia Quinn's Bridgerton series, Beverly Jenkins.

Contemporary: Nora Roberts, Susan Mallery, Jennifer Crusie.

Paranormal: Sherrilyn Kenyon, J.R. Ward — vampires, werewolves, demons as love interests.

Romantic suspense: Karen Robards, Tami Hoag.

LGBTQ+: T.J. Klune, Casey McQuiston, KJ Charles. A rapidly growing category.

Erotic romance: Sylvia Day, the post-Fifty Shades proliferation.

Each subgenre has dedicated readerships, conventions, and reader expectations. Authors who succeed in one don't always cross over.

concepts.title: Romance and Literary Respectability
concepts.contentHtml:
Romance has been the most consistently dismissed major genre. The dismissal — gendered (most readers and writers are women), formulaic (the HEA convention), commercial (volume of mass-market production) — has been increasingly contested.

Recent scholarship (Pamela Regis's A Natural History of the Romance Novel, 2003; the Journal of Popular Romance Studies) has taken the genre seriously on its own terms. Authors including Jennifer Weiner have publicly fought the literary world's dismissal.

Some 21st-century romance has crossed into literary acclaim: Casey McQuiston's Red, White & Royal Blue, Emily Henry's commercial-literary hybrids. The genre boundary, like other genre-literary boundaries, has weakened.

The basic point: romance does important emotional work for many millions of readers. Dismissing the genre because of its conventions is like dismissing the sonnet because it's 14 lines.
